title: Is It the Leader or the Team That Needs to Be Admired
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article reframes the idea of admiration in leadership, starting from the common assumption that leaders should aim to be admired by their teams. While acknowledging the real value of being admired — it builds trust and willingness to sacrifice — the piece argues that the most extraordinary leaders flip the emphasis: they focus on admiring their team rather than seeking admiration for themselves. The author contends that when leaders visibly admire the people they lead, team members feel empowered and work harder to remain worthy of that respect. The piece acknowledges admiration is ideally reciprocal, but insists that leaders should prioritize demonstrating admiration for their team over cultivating their own reputation, since the best leadership is always oriented around others.
points: Most leaders aspire to be admired by their team, believing it builds trust and credibility.
The most extraordinary leaders instead prioritize admiring their team rather than seeking admiration themselves.
When leaders visibly admire their team, members feel empowered to do their best work.
Team members work harder to remain worthy of a leader's demonstrated admiration.
For the best teams, admiration flows in both directions, but leaders should lead with admiring others first.
quotes: Leadership, for them, is always about the people they lead and not about themselves.
Leaders who are admired by their team members are conferred a credibility reserved for very few.
They believe it is more important for the leader to admire the team than it is for the team to admire the leader.
When leaders admire the team, and display that admiration, members feel empowered to do their best work and reach their highest potential.
In order not to diminish or lose that admiration, team members go above and beyond, proving every day that they are worthy of that respect.
The best leadership is always about others and not about the leader.
